questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Why a semiconductor conducts moderately
questions.learningObjective: Explain moderate conduction in semiconductors
questions.stem: Why does a semiconductor conduct only moderately at room temperature?

options.text: Only a few electrons have enough energy to cross the band gap.
The valence band is completely full and blocks current.
options.misconception: confuses full band with no conduction

options.text: The conduction band is completely empty at all times.
Impurities absorb all charge carriers immediately.

questions.explanation: Thermal energy promotes a small fraction of electrons across the band gap, giving moderate conduction. Full bands, empty bands, and impurity absorption are wrong causes.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Origin of an electron and hole pair
questions.learningObjective: Identify the origin of an electron-hole pair
questions.stem: What creates an electron-hole pair in an intrinsic semiconductor?

options.text: A donor atom donating an extra electron only.
Thermal promotion of an electron from valence to conduction band.
An acceptor atom creating a hole only.
Photon absorption at any energy always.

questions.explanation: Intrinsic pairs arise when thermal energy lifts an electron across the band gap, leaving a hole. Doping and arbitrary photon absorption are different processes.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: What a group five donor contributes
questions.learningObjective: State what a group-five donor contributes
questions.stem: What does a group-five donor contribute to a semiconductor?

answer.exemplar: A group-five donor contributes one extra electron to the conduction band, becoming a positive ion, and makes the material n-type with electrons as majority carriers.

questions.explanation: The fifth valence electron is loosely bound and becomes a conduction electron. The wrong idea is that it creates holes or stays bound.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: The depletion region at a junction
questions.learningObjective: Describe the depletion region at a junction
questions.stem: What happens in the depletion region of a p-n junction?

options.text: The region becomes highly conductive and shorts the junction.
Electrons and holes accumulate in large numbers there.
Mobile carriers diffuse away, leaving fixed ions and a field.
No electric field exists because charges cancel.

questions.explanation: Diffusion leaves fixed donor and acceptor ions, creating a depletion region and built-in field. Accumulation, conduction, and no field are wrong.

questions.stem: Which bias makes a p-n diode conduct easily?

options.text: Both biases conduct equally well.
Reverse bias, which widens the depletion region.
Zero bias, which removes the junction entirely.
Forward bias, which narrows the depletion region.

questions.explanation: Forward bias reduces the barrier and narrows depletion, allowing current. Reverse bias blocks current. Zero bias and equal conduction are wrong.

questions.topic: Current below the forward threshold

options.text: The diode is reverse biased at low voltage.
The barrier is still too high for significant diffusion.
The resistance becomes infinite below threshold.
The current flows only in the reverse direction.

questions.explanation: Below threshold the built-in barrier remains large, so only tiny leakage flows. Reverse bias, infinite resistance, and reverse current are wrong.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Reverse breakdown of a diode
questions.learningObjective: Explain reverse breakdown
questions.stem: What is reverse breakdown in a diode?

answer.exemplar: Reverse breakdown is the sharp increase in reverse current when the reverse voltage exceeds a critical value, either by avalanche multiplication or zener tunnelling.

questions.explanation: Beyond the critical reverse voltage, carriers multiply or tunnel and current rises sharply. The wrong idea is that the diode becomes an open circuit.

The transformer adds alternating noise to the output.
The diode leaks current in the reverse direction.
The output follows the rectified waveform between zero and peak.

questions.explanation: Without smoothing the output is the rectified waveform, rising and falling to zero each cycle. Transformer noise, leakage, and resistor storage are wrong causes.

It stores charge at peaks and supplies current between peaks.
It increases the peak voltage of the rectifier.
It short-circuits the alternating component to ground.

questions.explanation: The capacitor charges to the peak and discharges through the load between peaks, filling the gaps. Blocking DC, raising peak, and shorting AC are wrong.

questions.topic: Ripple from an unsmoothed rectifier
questions.learningObjective: Compute peak-to-peak ripple of unsmoothed rectifier
questions.stem: A rectifier peaks at 10 V with no smoothing; what is the peak-to-peak ripple in V?

answer.exemplar: The peak-to-peak ripple is 10 V, because the output swings from 0 to the 10 V peak each cycle.

questions.explanation: Without smoothing the output swings from 0 to peak, so ripple is 10 V. Half of peak or zero is wrong.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: How a filter capacitor smooths
questions.learningObjective: Relate capacitor size to ripple
questions.stem: If capacitance doubles, how does ripple voltage change?

options.text: It stays the same, because ripple depends only on load.
It doubles, because more capacitance stores more ripple.
It halves, because ripple is inversely proportional to C.
It becomes zero, because large C eliminates ripple.

questions.explanation: Ripple is inversely proportional to C, so doubling C halves ripple. Doubling, constant, and zero are wrong.
